role-targeting.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have "targeted a role" if your packet is a generic list of skills aimed at every job at once. A target you can send to any posting is not a target — it is a resume spray. Role targeting narrows the claim until each bullet points at one hiring bar.

role-targeting.text: A recruiter screen, six seconds per resume: yours says "passionate full-stack engineer, strong communicator, fast learner." The req wanted someone who has shipped payment infrastructure at scale — and nothing on your page proves you have. You get auto-rejected not because you cannot do the job, but because you never aimed the evidence at it.

Every application is a claim-versus-evidence match against one specific hiring bar, read under time pressure by a recruiter and then a panel. Role targeting converts "I am a good engineer" into "here is the exact proof this role demands" — Section 1 of the packet you carry through resumes, interviews, and negotiation.

role-targeting.prompt: "I want to work at a great company doing interesting work with modern tech." Before you polish that — what is wrong with it as a role target? Answer before reading on.
role-targeting.reveal: It aims at everyone, so it convinces no one. "Great / interesting / modern" are preferences, not a hiring bar, and none of them tell a reviewer which of your artifacts to weigh. A real target names the role, the seniority, and the two or three requirements the posting actually screens on — e.g. "Backend engineer, senior, must show production distributed-systems ownership and on-call incident response." The generic version feels ambitious while quietly guaranteeing your evidence lands on nothing.

role-targeting.subtitle: The hiring bar (from the posting) is decomposed into requirements; each requirement is matched to one of YOUR artifacts. Matched edges are proof; the unmatched requirement is the gap the packet must name. Recruiter screen and panel read this map, not your intentions.

storyboard.say: Start with one job posting. Not every job — one. This is the single hiring bar you're aiming at.
Decompose that posting into its must-have requirements — the concrete things the role actually demands.
Each requirement enters the proof map carrying one question: what evidence proves you meet it?
Now pull in your artifacts — shipped work, not adjectives — and match each one to a requirement it proves.
Any requirement with no matching artifact gets flagged: this is the unproven gap the packet must name honestly.
The recruiter screen and panel read the matched proof — six seconds against evidence, not against your intentions.
The invariant: every claim points at one hiring bar. A target, backed by artifacts — never a spray of adjectives.

role-targeting.text: The senior tell in targeting is naming your own gap before the interviewer finds it. A portfolio claim is more credible when it ties to an artifact — so "here is the one requirement I cannot yet prove, and here is the adjacent evidence closest to it" reads as calibration, not weakness. (SWEBOK V4 is a body-of-knowledge catalog, not a hiring rubric; do not cite it as 'grounding' this framing.) The candidate who hides the gap gets caught; the one who names it controls the conversation.

role-targeting.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this packet is aimed at THIS role, not a happy-path answer." Which packet passes?
options: One that lists every skill the candidate has, so no requirement is ever missed.
One that names the role and its must-have requirements, maps each to a specific inspectable artifact, and honestly flags the one requirement it cannot prove.
One with a polished summary paragraph describing the candidate as passionate and versatile.
One that claims the candidate is a strong fit for the role, backed by years of experience.
role-targeting.explanation: Only option 2 ties claims to a specific hiring bar AND to artifacts a reviewer can open, and it names the gap instead of hiding it — the difference between targeted proof and a happy-path answer. The exhaustive skill list (1) is a spray; the summary paragraph (3) and the "strong fit" assertion (4) are claims about the candidate with no artifact behind them.

market-scan.doNotClaim: Do not claim you "scanned the market" if you read one dream job post and pattern-matched yourself onto it. One posting is an anecdote, not a signal. And do not map a requirement to evidence you cannot show under a walkthrough — an aspiration is not an artifact.

market-scan.text: Two engineers apply for the same senior role. One writes a resume from memory and lists what she is proud of. The other reads twelve live postings, sees "owns on-call and incident response" in nine of them, and leads her packet with the outage she ran. Same skills, one recruiter screen survives — because one aimed at the market and the other aimed at a mirror.

This is the foundation move of the whole Interview & Portfolio track: before you rewrite a single resume bullet or story, you find out what the market is actually paying for. The Market Scan turns "here is everything I have done" into "here is the evidence this role is screening for" — Section 1 of the packet you carry through every later lesson.

market-scan.prompt: "I have five years of experience, so I'll list all my skills and let the recruiter pick." Before you build a resume that way — what's wrong with it as a strategy? Answer before reading on.
market-scan.reveal: It outsources the targeting to a stranger reading 300 resumes in an afternoon. A recruiter screen lasts about six seconds and pattern-matches your top lines against the requirements they were handed. If your evidence is unranked, the thing they need is buried at position nine. The scan inverts it: you rank YOUR evidence by what the market repeats, so the first line they read is the one they were sent to find. Listing everything feels thorough while quietly deciding nothing.

# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet

## 1. Market Scan
- Target role: Senior Backend Engineer (payments) · scanned 11 postings · 2026-06
- REQ (9/11) Owns on-call + incident response  -> artifact: postmortem_checkout_outage.md      confidence: strong
- REQ (8/11) Designs + ships REST/gRPC services -> artifact: orders-service repo + design_doc.md  confidence: strong
- REQ (7/11) Production SQL at scale            -> story: cut p99 query 4s->300ms (STAR ready)    confidence: mid
- REQ (5/11) Kafka / event-driven experience    -> GAP: only a side project, no prod traffic       confidence: gap
- Rejected framing: leading with "React + CSS" (0/11 asked; my strongest but off-target)
- Boundary: salary band + remote policy tracked separately, do NOT rank evidence by them
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.
Name the target + the sample: One role, a real count, a date. "Scanned 11 postings" is the difference between a signal and a hunch — and it lets a reviewer check you.
The strong claims, mapped: The two requirements that recur most, each pointing at a named, inspectable artifact. These lead the resume and the recruiter screen.
A story, not just an artifact: Evidence can be a STAR story with a number in it (4s to 300ms), not only a repo. Mark it mid-confidence until you have rehearsed the walkthrough.
Name the gap honestly: 7/11 wanted Kafka; you have a side project, not prod traffic. Marking it GAP routes it to repair — it must NOT become a padded resume bullet.
The rejected framing: Your strongest skill (React) appeared in 0/11 postings for this role. Leading with it feels good and targets nothing. Naming what you cut is the discipline.
The scope boundary: Salary and remote policy matter — but if they rank your evidence, you optimize the packet for the wrong thing. Track them; do not let them drive.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

storyboard.say: Start with eight to twelve real, live postings for the same role — not your memory of what the job wants.
Read across the postings, not down any single one, and extract the must-haves each role actually screens for.
Count how often each requirement repeats across postings — that frequency becomes the demand signal.
Salary and perks stay out: they inform your choice, but they must not drive how requirements get ranked.
Now rank requirements top-down by frequency and map each one to a named artifact or story you own.
On a match, the requirement joins your evidence packet — every claim pointing to something inspectable.
On no match, it becomes a gap — routed to skill repair, never faked onto the resume.
The result: not everything you've done, but the exact evidence this role is screening for — Section 1 of your packet.

## 1. Positioning
- Role target: Senior Backend Engineer (latency / infra-heavy JD)

# Writing Section 1 of the packet, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real project you have shipped and write a role-targeted portfolio claim + resume bullet whose every phrase points at a named artifact — then defend it under one recruiter objection. Positioning, not decoration: the claim names the proof, never just the topic.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only score_bullet at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your bullet aloud. If it starts with "Responsible for" or "Worked on," you named a seat, not a result — rewrite it to lead with the impact.
# 2. Point to the number. If there is no quantified result (percent, dollars, time, scale), a reviewer has nothing to challenge and nothing to be impressed by — add it or cut the claim.
# 3. Open the artifact link map: every load-bearing phrase must map to one openable artifact (report, PR, dashboard, demo). Any phrase with no artifact is a topic — link it or delete it.
# 4. Run the recruiter-screen test: hand Section 1 to someone outside the project and ask them to restate what you did, how much, and where to verify. If they can't, the positioning is vague, not them.
# 5. Check the role target: the same project should read differently for a different JD. If your bullet is identical for every role, you positioned nothing — you just described the work.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

VERBS = {"cut", "reduced", "shipped", "built", "led", "designed", "migrated"}

BULLETS = [
    "Worked on search infrastructure and helped with performance",
    "Cut p99 search latency 4.1s to 900ms (-78%), load-test report + PR linked",
    "Passionate team player with strong communication skills",
    "Migrated 14 services to the new auth gateway, zero rollbacks, memo linked",
    "Improved database performance significantly",
]

MARKERS = ["PR", "report", "dashboard", "repo", "memo"]


def score_bullet(text):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied career fixtures.
    # Return inspectable evidence; do not invent experience, outcomes, or market data.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

def pct_reduction(old, new):
    return round((old - new) / old * 100)


for b in BULLETS:
    score, missing = score_bullet(b)
    tag = "KEEP" if score == 3 else "REWRITE"
    lack = ','.join(missing) if missing else 'none'
    print(f"[{score}/3] {tag} missing={lack} :: {b[:46]}")
print(f"honest improvement: {pct_reduction(4.1, 0.9)}% reduction")
print(f"resume-lie version would claim: {round((4.1 - 0.9) / 0.9 * 100)}%")

storyboard.say: It starts with raw project work — real effort, but shapeless, nobody can tell what it proves yet.
You aim it at a specific role, and that target tunes which result the claim should emphasize.
The raw work gets rewritten as a result — a numbered outcome — and becomes your portfolio claim.
The invariant: that claim must link to an evidence artifact — a load-test report a reader can actually open.
The same claim compresses into a resume bullet and expands into an interview story — all three point at one proof.
The recruiter skims the bullet; when it carries a number and a link, it survives the six-second screen.
The dashed path is the failure: an unverifiable claim, a topic you named with no artifact, gets cut in six seconds.

linkedin-github-positioning.prompt: Your GitHub profile shows 47 public repos, most half-finished tutorials. Is that a strength ('look how much I build') or a liability? Answer before reading on.
linkedin-github-positioning.reveal: A liability. A recruiter screen samples, not audits — she opens the top of your profile, and 47 unpinned repos means the first thing she sees is a forked tutorial, not your best work. Volume without curation reads as noise. Positioning is subtraction: 3 pinned repos that each prove one claim beat 47 that prove you follow along. What you leave unpinned is a decision, not an accident.

linkedin-github-positioning.subtitle: A recruiter's eye moves headline → pinned repo → README, taking the failure path (unpinned tutorial, no README, dead claim) or the repair path (role-targeted, pinned proof, claim → artifact).

nodes.label: Tab closed

legend.label: the three decision gates in the screen

storyboard.say: A recruiter with 40 tabs open lands on your profile. She has six seconds, and her eye goes straight to the headline.
If it reads 'aspiring developer passionate about tech', she learns nothing about your role. Tab closed before your best work loads.
The repair: make the role unmistakable. A clear headline earns the next glance instead of the close button.
Her eye drops to pinned repos. If your top repo is a course fork, the signal dies and she bounces again.
Curated pinned repos survive: she opens pinned number one, the piece of proof you chose to put first.
Inside, a claim with no README, no demo, no commit is a dead claim. No artifact means the tab closes.
But when the claim points at an artifact she can open, it holds under inspection and you pass the screen.
The invariant: no claim without an artifact. A skill you cannot show is a skill you cannot claim.

linkedin-github-positioning.code:
# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet

## Positioning (role target: Backend Engineer — Python/APIs)
- LinkedIn headline: Backend Engineer · Python & FastAPI · shipped a 12k-req/day inventory API
- About hook (3 lines): I build backend services that stay up under load.
  Most recent: rebuilt an inventory sync that cut stale-stock errors 90%.
  Proof, not adjectives — every claim below links to the code.
- Pinned repo: github.com/me/inventory-sync  (pinned #1, not 'aspiring')
- Claim → artifact map:
    "handles 12k req/day"  -> README#load-test  (k6 run, p99 chart)
    "cut stale-stock 90%"  -> README#before-after (metric + commit a3f9c1)
    "idempotent retries"   -> src/sync.py#L40-88  (the dedup key)
- Resume bullet: Cut stale-stock errors 90% by making inventory sync idempotent (Python/FastAPI, 12k req/day).

steps.label: Name the role target
steps.note: Positioning starts with ONE role. 'Backend Engineer — Python/APIs' aims every claim below it. A packet with no role target is a bio, not positioning.

steps.label: The headline is a proof, not a vibe
steps.note: 'Backend Engineer · shipped a 12k-req/day API' says role + evidence in one line. 'Passionate about tech' says nothing a recruiter can screen on.

steps.label: About hook = 3 lines, quantified
steps.note: Lead with what you build, then the most recent proof with a number. The recruiter screen samples the top — front-load the strongest metric.

steps.label: Pin, don't dump
steps.note: One pinned repo that proves the target role beats 47 unpinned. Pinning is the curation decision the pretest was about.

steps.label: The claim → artifact map
steps.note: The heart of positioning: each claim points at something openable — a README anchor, a chart, a commit hash, a line range. A claim with no artifact gets cut, not softened.

steps.label: Compress to a resume bullet
steps.note: Same proof, one line: verb + quantified result + how + stack. This bullet is reused verbatim on the resume and in the interview story.

linkedin-github-positioning.caption: Positioning is not writing better adjectives. It is deleting the claims you cannot prove and pinning the ones you can.

linkedin-github-positioning.text: The senior tell: strong engineers position with numbers a skeptic could verify, not adjectives a fan would applaud. 'Passionate, hard-working, team player' is unfalsifiable — it survives on every profile, so it distinguishes none. 'Cut p99 latency from 4s to 800ms' can be checked, so it carries weight. If a competitor could copy your headline word-for-word without lying, it is not positioning. This mirrors the general engineering principle of grounding a claim in verifiable evidence, not assertion. (SWEBOK V4 covers verification/validation of software artifacts; it does not make the stated claim about 'engineering claims,' so do not attribute this framing to it.)

linkedin-github-positioning.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Your profile says you can build scalable APIs — prove it, don't tell me.' Which response is real positioning, not a happy-path answer?
options: "I'm passionate about scalable systems and I learn fast, so I'd pick it up quickly."
"Pinned repo #1: a FastAPI service; README#load-test has the k6 run showing p99 under 200ms at 12k req/day, and commit a3f9c1 is where I made retries idempotent."
"I have 47 repos on GitHub, so clearly I build a lot."
"My headline lists FastAPI, Postgres, Redis, Docker, Kubernetes, and more."
linkedin-github-positioning.explanation: Only option 2 answers 'prove it' with an inspectable artifact chain: a pinned repo, a README section with a load-test chart, and a specific commit. Option 1 is unfalsifiable adjectives; option 3 is volume, not curation; option 4 is a skills salad — a technology list is inventory, not evidence a claim is true. Positioning ties every claim to something a skeptic can open.

linkedin-github-positioning.intro: Prove your positioning holds — no vibes:
items: Read your headline aloud. If a competitor with your background could copy it word-for-word without lying, it is a vibe, not positioning — add a quantified proof.
For every claim on the profile, name the artifact a reviewer would open (README anchor, chart, commit, line range). Any claim with no artifact gets cut, not softened.
Check the role target is explicit: a stranger reads your headline + About and can name the job you want in one guess.
Confirm your best repo is pinned #1 and its README opens with proof, not a one-liner — the recruiter screen samples the top.
Confirm the resume bullet and the interview story reuse the same quantified claim, so your proof is consistent across every surface.

prompts: In your own words: why does a technologies list ('Python, React, Docker...') read as inventory, and what turns it into positioning?
Explain the claim → artifact map using your own pinned repo: pick one claim and name exactly what a recruiter would open to verify it.
What is your explicit role target, and which repos did you deliberately NOT pin — and why is leaving them off a positioning decision, not laziness?

portfolio-proof-map.unlock: Every phrase in your portfolio claim points at a specific, inspectable artifact — no claim floats without a link.
portfolio-proof-map.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a proof map if your claim is a topic ("worked on search relevance") instead of a proof ("cut p99 search latency 4s→900ms, PR #418, dashboard link"). Naming the topic is a description; naming the artifact + result is proof. A claim a reviewer cannot click is not on the map.

portfolio-proof-map.text: The recruiter screen is over in ninety seconds: your résumé says "improved performance," and the interviewer asks "show me exactly what you did and how you know it worked." You reach for a link — and there isn't one. Two candidates built the same feature; only one turned it into evidence a stranger could verify in a single click.

A portfolio is not a gallery of things you touched — it is a proof system where every claim is bonded to an artifact and a defensible story. The Proof Map is the artifact you carry through the whole Interview & Portfolio arc: role targeting, résumé bullets, the recruiter screen, and the technical walkthrough all read off it.

portfolio-proof-map.prompt: "Built a scalable microservices platform using React, Node, Kubernetes, and GraphQL." Before you polish the wording — what is wrong with that as portfolio proof? Answer before reading on.
portfolio-proof-map.reveal: It is a keyword list wearing a claim's clothes. It names technologies but proves nothing: no result, no artifact, no way for a reviewer to check that YOU did any of it. A recruiter can't tell your contribution from your team's, and an interviewer has nothing to open. The proof version replaces the stack with a bonded claim: "Cut checkout p99 from 4s to 900ms (SLO 1s) by adding a read-through cache — PR #418, before/after Grafana panel, load-test transcript." Same work; one is searchable by ATS and unfalsifiable, the other is evidence.

# Portfolio Proof Packet — Checkout Latency

## Role target
- Aiming at: Backend / Platform Engineer (mid) — bar: owns a measurable prod win end-to-end

## Portfolio claim (bonded)
- Claim: Cut checkout p99 latency 4.0s -> 0.9s (SLO 1s) for 100% of orders
- Artifact map:
  - what I changed  -> PR #418 (read-through cache on order-summary)
  - it worked       -> Grafana panel "checkout-p99" before/after (link)
  - it is safe      -> load-test transcript + rollback note in PR description

## Interview story (STAR)
- Situation: p99 was 4s against a 1s SLO; VP wanted it "fixed by Friday"
- Task: find the real cause, ship a reversible fix without daytime downtime
- Action: profiled -> recompute on read, not writes; added read-through cache; guarded with TTL + invalidation
- Result: 4.0s -> 0.9s, zero incidents, PR #418 merged, dashboard shows the drop

## Résumé bullet (one line)
- Cut checkout p99 latency 78% (4.0s->0.9s) via read-through caching; PR + dashboard on request

## Recruiter-screen line (90s)
- "I owned a latency fix that took checkout from 4s to under 1s — I can show the PR and the before/after graph"

## Reviewer objection + repair
- Objection: "How do we know the cache isn't serving stale orders?"
- Repair: invalidation-on-write test in PR #418; link the test, not a promise

## Capstone connection
- Reuse in career readiness packet: this is proof #1 in the story bank
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.
Role target sets the bar: Before writing a claim, name the role. The bar for a platform role ("owns a measurable prod win") is what makes "cut latency 78%" land instead of "helped with performance."
The claim is a result, not a topic: Quantified and scoped: 4.0s→0.9s, SLO named, coverage stated. "Improved performance" would be a topic; a number a reviewer can verify is proof.

The artifact map — the whole skill: Every phrase of the claim points at an inspectable thing: the change (PR), the result (dashboard), the safety (load test). This is the bond. No line here means no proof.
STAR turns the claim into a defense: Situation/Task/Action/Result so the story survives "walk me through it." The Action names the real cause you found, not the tools you used.

Two derived surfaces from one claim: The résumé bullet and the recruiter line are compressions of the SAME bonded claim — so ATS keyword, screen pitch, and deep-dive all agree and all trace to PR #418.
Pre-load the objection: Name the reviewer's hardest question and answer it with a linked test, not a promise. An objection you raised first can't ambush you in the room.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

A peer reads it and can name the exact evidence behind each claim without you narrating.

# Writing the proof packet, one field at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real project you built and write the Portfolio Proof Map: a role-targeted portfolio claim, the exact artifact each phrase points to, and the interview story that defends it under pressure. The output is a reviewable packet, not a note.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only proof_density at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your portfolio claim aloud. Every clause must point at a specific artifact (PR, commit, dashboard, doc). If any clause has no link, it is a topic — bond it or cut it.
# 2. Confirm the claim is quantified and scoped: a number, a baseline, and who/how-much it affected — not "improved" or "scalable."
# 3. Hand the packet to a peer and have them open one artifact and restate what YOU did. If they can't separate your work from the team's, tighten the claim.
# 4. Check the STAR story's Action names the real cause you addressed, not the tools you used. Tools are not a contribution.
# 5. Confirm you pre-loaded the reviewer's hardest objection and answered it with a linked test or transcript, not a promise.
# 6. Verify the résumé bullet and the recruiter-screen line are compressions of the SAME bonded claim, so all three surfaces trace to the same artifact.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

CLAIMS = {
    "checkout-retry": [
        "rebuilt-retry-path",
        "dup-charges-cut-93pct",
        "p95-under-300ms",
        "industry-leading-reliability",
    ],
    "auth-migration": [
        "migrated-14-services",
        "zero-rollbacks",
    ],
    "search-latency": [
        "p99-4.1s-to-900ms",
        "30pct-of-queries",
        "saved-oncall-hours",
    ],
}

LINKS = {
    "rebuilt-retry-path": "pr:#188",
    "dup-charges-cut-93pct": "dashboard-export:dup-charges-45-to-3-per-wk",
    "p95-under-300ms": "loadtest:k6-p95-287ms",
    "migrated-14-services": "repo:auth-gateway-migration",
    "zero-rollbacks": "dashboard-export:deploy-log-90d",
    "p99-4.1s-to-900ms": "loadtest:before-after-report",
    "30pct-of-queries": "pr:#214-description",
}


def proof_density(claims, links):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied career fixtures.
    # Return inspectable evidence; do not invent experience, outcomes, or market data.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

per_claim, overall, floating = proof_density(CLAIMS, LINKS)
for name, anchored, total in per_claim:
    print(f"{name}: {anchored}/{total} clauses anchored")
print(f"overall proof density: {overall}%")
print(f"floating clauses: {', '.join(floating)}")

search-latency: 2/3 clauses anchored

storyboard.say: Everything starts with the role you're targeting — the role sets the bar for what your portfolio claims have to clear.
Each portfolio claim is a load-bearing promise, and the rule is simple: it must bond to an inspectable artifact.
That artifact is what backs your résumé bullet — the line a recruiter skims now has a clickable thing behind it.
The same artifact backs the recruiter screen, so when they ask 'show me,' you reach for a link that actually exists.
Every claim is also defended by an interview story — the result, and how you'd tell it under questioning.
That story is what holds under pressure in the technical walkthrough, where a stranger probes exactly what you did.
The dashed path is the failure: a claim with no artifact goes straight into the walkthrough and collapses.
The invariant: no claim without a clickable artifact. A claim a reviewer can't inspect is a topic, not proof.

# Case Study: Cut checkout p95 latency 60% under a no-downtime constraint

## Portfolio claim (the resume bullet)
Cut checkout p95 latency 800ms -> 320ms (60%) by moving cart pricing to a
read replica + cache, with zero daytime downtime on the primary revenue path.

## STAR interview story
- Situation: Black-Friday load doubled; checkout p95 breached the 500ms SLO.
- Task: bring p95 under SLO without taking the checkout path down.
- Action: profiled -> pricing recompute was the hot path; added a read replica
  + a 30s cache; shipped behind a flag; rolled out 5% -> 100%.
- Result: p95 800ms -> 320ms; SLO green; 0 downtime; +2.1% conversion.

## Artifact link map (every claim -> one inspectable artifact)
- "800ms -> 320ms": Grafana panel /d/chk-latency + load-test report PR #412
- "read replica + cache": PR #418 (diff), ADR-014 (why cache TTL = 30s)
- "0 downtime": deploy log + flag-rollout dashboard 5%->100%
- "+2.1% conversion": experiment readout exp-2291

## Selected vs rejected approach
- Selected: replica + short-TTL cache (reversible, no schema change).
- Rejected: denormalize pricing into orders table -> irreversible migration,
  violates no-downtime constraint. Reversal condition: if cache staleness
  causes >0.1% mispriced carts, kill cache, fall back to primary.

## Expected failure + verification method
- Feared failure: stale cache serves a wrong price to a paying customer.
- Verification: contract test asserts cached price == primary price within TTL;
  synthetic canary re-prices 100 carts/min and alerts on mismatch.

## Reviewer objection + repair notes
- Objection: "60% could be noise — how do you know the cache caused it?"
- Repair: link the flag on/off A/B split, not just the before/after; the 5%
  cohort isolates the cause. (Added exp-2291 split to the link map.)

## Capstone connection
- Reused as the flagship case study in career_readiness_packet.md.
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.
The portfolio claim: The resume bullet, but quantified with a before AND an after (800ms -> 320ms), the constraint named. A bare "improved latency" has nothing for the link map to point at.
The STAR story (for humans): Situation, Task, Action, Result — the recruiter screen and behavioral round read this. Result carries numbers, not adjectives. This is the story on top.

The artifact link map (for engineers): The load-bearing part. Every quantified claim above maps to ONE inspectable artifact — a PR, a dashboard, an ADR, an experiment. This is what the technical walkthrough clicks. No claim floats free.

Selected vs rejected + reversal: Naming the rejected option (irreversible migration) and WHY you rejected it is the senior tell — it proves judgment, not just execution. The reversal condition proves you knew the risk.
Expected failure + verification: The realistic production failure (stale price to a paying customer) and the proof that catches it. A case study with no named failure reads as luck.

Reviewer objection + repair: Pre-answer the sharpest objection ("is the number noise?") and repair the packet before the interview finds the hole. The A/B split beats the before/after because it isolates cause.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

storyboard.say: One shipped project can take two fates in an interview. Everything starts here, with real work you actually did.
Take the top path first: the project becomes a bare claim, a single resume bullet with nothing under it.
The claim reads fine, so it sails through the recruiter screen and advances toward the deep dive.
Then the technical walkthrough asks: walk me through it. With no evidence under the sentence, it collapses.
Now the repair path. From the same project, build the case study, a defense packet where every claim binds to an artifact.
When an objection comes, the packet answers it: each claim maps to a commit, PR, dashboard, or decision record.
The artifact holds under pressure, and the objection turns into credible evidence you can defend all the way through.
Same project, two fates. A claim floats free and collapses; a claim bound to evidence survives every round.

project-case-studies.text: The senior tell in a case study is the rejected approach. Anyone can narrate what they built; naming what they deliberately did NOT build — and why it violated a constraint — is what separates "I executed a ticket" from "I made a judgment call." SWEBOK V4 frames engineering design as tradeoff decisions under competing constraints, not code volume. (SWEBOK describes, it does not 'grade'; and drop the ABET co-attribution unless separately verified.) Your packet should read that way.

project-case-studies.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this case study is not just a happy-path story you polished for the interview." What is the strongest response?
options: Re-tell the STAR story with more confidence and more detail.
Point to the artifact link map, the named expected failure with its verification method, and the rejected approach with its reversal condition.
Say the project was on a team so the details are fuzzy but it definitely worked.
Add more impressive-sounding metrics to the portfolio claim.
project-case-studies.explanation: The reviewer is testing whether evidence exists under the story. Only option 2 points to inspectable proof: the link map binds each claim to an artifact, the named failure + verification shows you engineered for the unhappy path, and the rejected option + reversal condition shows judgment under constraint. Re-telling with confidence (1), hedging (3), and inflating metrics (4) all add words while adding zero evidence — the exact failure mode the packet exists to kill.

behavioral-story-bank.text: The interviewer says 'Tell me about a time you handled a hard technical problem,' and you feel your whole career blur into 'um, well, there was this one bug…' — while the candidate before you told a 90-second story with a number in it and a link to the PR. Same work. One had a story bank; one had a memory.

A recruiter screen and a behavioral round are search through your past for evidence, under time pressure. The story bank converts 'I did a lot of things' into a small set of retrievable, artifact-backed stories you can fire on demand — the core section of the interview-defense packet you carry into the capstone.

behavioral-story-bank.prompt: 'I refactored the billing service and it got way better.' Before you polish the wording — what is wrong with that as an interview story? Answer before reading on.
behavioral-story-bank.reveal: It is a claim with no evidence and no shape. 'Way better' names no baseline, no result, no artifact — the interviewer can't tell effort from impact. The gold version has a spine (Situation → Task → Action → Result) AND a number AND a link: 'p99 checkout latency was 4.2s against a 1s SLO (Situation/Task); I traced it to N+1 loads and batched them (Action); p99 dropped to 780ms, here's the PR (Result).' # Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet
## Target role: Backend Engineer (latency-sensitive systems)

## Story 1 — "The 4-second checkout"
- Situation: p99 checkout-confirm latency was 4.2s against a 1s SLO; ~2% cart abandonment tied to it
- Task: I owned the confirm endpoint; mandate = get p99 under 1s without daytime downtime
- Action: profiled the request, found an N+1 loading line items per order, batched into one query + added a covering index
- Result: p99 4.2s -> 780ms (81% cut); abandonment on that step -0.9pt over 2 weeks
- Artifact: PR #1487 (before/after flamegraph) + Grafana panel "checkout_p99" (link)

## Resume bullet (compressed Result-first)
- Cut p99 checkout latency 4.2s -> 780ms (81%) by eliminating an N+1 query; recovered ~0.9pt of step abandonment

## Objection + response
- Objection: "How do you know the drop wasn't just lower traffic that week?"
- Response: latency fell the deploy hour, not gradually; the Grafana panel shows the step-change at deploy T0 with flat request volume

## Repair note
- First draft said "we improved latency" — no baseline, no owner. Repaired to a solo Action + a baseline + a linked panel.
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.
Situation carries the baseline: A number the reviewer can anchor on (4.2s vs a 1s SLO). No baseline means the Result has nothing to be measured against.
Task names YOUR mandate: 'I owned the confirm endpoint.' Behavioral rounds probe for 'I' vs 'we' — the Task line is where you claim the surface you're accountable for.
Action is specific and solo: 'Profiled, found the N+1, batched + indexed.' Name the actual technical move. 'Optimized it' is a claim; 'batched an N+1' is evidence you understood the cause.
Result is quantified two ways: A technical number (781ms) AND a business number (-0.9pt abandonment). One proves competence, the other proves you know why it mattered.
Artifact = the link map: PR + dashboard panel. This is the line that turns the story from a claim into inspectable evidence — the whole point of the bank.
Objection pre-loads the defense: Anticipate 'was it luck?' and answer it with the artifact (step-change at deploy, flat traffic). You defend the Result before they attack it.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

A recruiter reads one story and can restate what you did and what changed — without you narrating.

# Writing one bank entry, line by line
#
# Mission: Take one real project you shipped and build a Behavioral Story Bank: three STAR-structured interview stories, each mapped to a concrete artifact, a resume bullet, and a reviewer objection with a repair — all inside portfolio_story_and_interview_defense_packet.md.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only coverage at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Every story has all four STAR parts. If you can't say the Task in one 'I'-sentence, you haven't claimed a surface — fix it.
# 2. Every Result has a number with a baseline (from X to Y), not an adjective ('a lot', 'significantly').
# 3. Every story links to one artifact a reviewer can actually open — a PR, dashboard, doc, or commit. No link = not bankable yet.
# 4. Each story has a resume bullet that leads with the Result, compressed to one line a recruiter scans in 3 seconds.
# 5. At least one story has a pre-loaded objection + response that rules out luck or 'the team did it' — and you can defend it from the artifact.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

COMPETENCIES = [
    "conflict", "failure", "ambiguity", "leadership",
    "delivery-under-pressure", "data-driven-decisions",
]

STORIES = {
    "ttl-disagreement": {
        "covers": {"conflict", "data-driven-decisions", "leadership",
                    "delivery-under-pressure"},
        "has_number": True, "has_artifact": True,
    },
    "retry-storm-incident": {
        "covers": {"delivery-under-pressure"},
        "has_number": True, "has_artifact": True,
    },
    "search-migration": {
        "covers": {"ambiguity"},
        "has_number": False, "has_artifact": True,
    },
}


def coverage(stories, competencies):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied career fixtures.
    # Return inspectable evidence; do not invent experience, outcomes, or market data.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

uncovered, overloaded, unquantified = coverage(STORIES, COMPETENCIES)
print(f"uncovered competencies: {', '.join(uncovered)}")
print(f"overloaded story: {overloaded[0]} carries {overloaded[1]} competencies")
print(f"stories not proof-grade: {', '.join(unquantified)}")
print(f"bank verdict: {len(uncovered)} gaps to fill before the loop")

uncovered competencies: failure
overloaded story: ttl-disagreement carries 4 competencies
stories not proof-grade: search-migration

storyboard.say: Every bank entry starts with Situation: the context you were dropped into, the stakes that made this worth telling.
Situation sets up the Task — your specific charge — which in turn drives the Action, the concrete moves only you can claim.
Action produces the Result — and this is a decision point: a strong Result carries a number, a weak one is just a feeling.
One entry, one spine: Situation, Task, Action, Result — the same story feeds your interview answer, resume bullet, and screen.
The Result must be verified by an Artifact — a PR, dashboard, or doc a reviewer can open. No artifact means unverifiable.
Under pressure the interviewer raises an Objection that attacks the Result — 'was that really your impact, or the team's?'
The Artifact answers the Objection: the link is the evidence that settles the doubt on the spot.
If the Result can't survive the objection, route it back for repair — re-quantify or re-anchor before the story earns its slot.

# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet

## Context
- Project: Checkout flow for a side-project storefront (Next.js + Stripe)
- My role: sole engineer; owned the payment path end to end

## Decision
- Selected: webhook-confirmed orders (mark PAID only on Stripe's `payment_intent.succeeded` webhook)
- Rejected: client-side confirmation (mark PAID when the browser returns from Stripe)
- Why: a dropped connection after payment must NOT lose a real, paid order

## Expected failure (the one I feared)
- Customer pays, closes the tab before redirect -> order silently never recorded -> money taken, nothing shipped

## Verification
- Test: simulated a dropped redirect; webhook still fired; order recorded PAID (link: tests/checkout.webhook.test.ts)
- Evidence: PR #47 (the flow) + Stripe dashboard event log + funnel before/after

## Reviewer objection + answer
- Objection: "Webhooks add latency and a failure mode of their own."
- Answer: idempotent handler keyed on payment_intent.id; ret/replay is safe (link: PR #47 handler)

## Resume bullet
- Rebuilt checkout on webhook-confirmed orders, closing a race that could take payment without recording the sale (PR #47)

## Capstone connection
- Reused in the career capstone as the flagship story in the story bank

The failure you feared: Specific enough to picture: 'money taken, nothing shipped'. This is what makes the decision matter — it defends against a real, nameable harm.
Verification (the anti-vibes gate): How you KNOW it worked, with links. A test that simulates the dropped redirect is proof; 'it worked when I tried it' is a vibe.

Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

# Mission: Take one real project you built and write portfolio_story_and_interview_defense_packet.md: a technical explanation of what you built and why, tied claim-by-claim to inspectable artifacts, plus the STAR interview story and the one-line resume bullet that survive a recruiter screen and a technical walkthrough under pressure.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only analyze at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your resume bullet aloud. If it names only tools ('React, Node, Postgres') and no decision or outcome, it is a stack recital — rewrite it around the call you made.
# 2. For every claim in the packet, name the artifact it links to (PR, test, dashboard, doc). If any claim has no link, it is floating — attach proof or cut it.

# 4. Point to the failure case in your verification. If your only evidence is the happy path, a reviewer's 'how do you know?' will break it.

    "The replay caught 4801 of 4812 duplicates (see replay-report)",
    "It fails open on redis outage so notifications never drop",
    "That eliminated the duplicate-push complaints entirely",
]


def analyze(sentences):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied career fixtures.
    # Return inspectable evidence; do not invent experience, outcomes, or market data.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

claims, anchored, decision_pos, density = analyze(EXPLANATION)

print(f"first decision at sentence: {decision_pos}")

verdict = "decision-first" if 0 < decision_pos <= 2 else "buried decision"
print(f"structure: {verdict}")

storyboard.say: It starts with the project — real work you did that a stranger has never seen.
You distill that project into a defense packet: the single source of truth you can stand behind under pressure.
From that one packet you derive three artifacts: one resume line, one STAR story, one portfolio claim.
The invariant: each of those three must point back at the same artifact — the evidence a reviewer can open.
Here is the failure path: a claim ships with no link, and it drifts off as a floating claim.
The repair is simple — attach the proof, and the floating claim reconnects to the artifact.
The lesson: no claim without an artifact. A claim with a link is proof; a claim without one is just a story.

# System Design Defense Packet — URL Shortener
## 1. Context + assumptions
- Scope: read-heavy (100:1 reads:writes), 10k redirects/sec peak, <100ms p99
- Hard constraint: redirect must never 404 a valid code (data loss = trust loss)
## 2. Selected approach
- Cache-aside: App reads Redis; on miss, load from KV, populate, redirect
## 3. Rejected approach
- Write-through everything to cache: rejected — memory cost + cold-start floods KV
## 4. Expected failure (the break)
- Cache eviction after deploy -> miss storm -> KV overwhelmed -> p99 spikes to 4s
## 5. Verification method (the proof)
- Load test: warm vs cold cache; assert p99 < 100ms warm, KV QPS bounded on cold
## 6. Reviewer objection + response
- "What at 10x?" -> shard KV by code prefix; request-coalesce misses (single-flight)
## 7. Repair notes
- Add negative-cache + jittered TTL so evictions don't expire in lockstep
## 8. Resume bullet (claim -> artifact)
- "Designed a 10k-rps redirect path; killed a cache-miss-storm failure — see packet"

system-design-interview.subtitle: Six components on the write → read path. The suspect edge (App → Cache → KV Store) is where the tradeoff and the failure live: a cache miss storm hammering the key-value store. Analytics is deliberately out of scope.

legend.label: the suspect hot path (where the tradeoff lives)
blast radius: cache miss storm floods the KV store
out of scope — defended, not forgotten

storyboard.say: A redirect request enters here: the client asks GET /abc123, and the load balancer routes it to an app server.
The app server takes the hot path first, checking the cache for the short code before it ever touches durable storage.
On a cache miss it loads the mapping from the KV store, the source of truth for every short-code-to-URL pair.
Here is the suspect edge: at ten times traffic a miss storm floods App to Cache to KV, and the key-value store buckles.
The app returns a 301 straight from the KV truth, then fires analytics fire-and-forget so logging never blocks the redirect.
The insight: don't tour components, defend one arrow. Name the miss-storm failure, cite the metric, say how you'd know.

A portfolio claim only converts when it survives inspection: the artifact, the tradeoff you rejected, the failure you feared, and the proof it works. The Coding Interview Loop turns 'I understand the project' into 'here is a decision I framed, built, broke, and defended — read it' — the evidence packet you carry into every screen, walkthrough, and negotiation.

coding-interview-loop.prompt: 'I built a caching layer that improved performance by 40%.' Strong resume bullet? Before you agree — what does a senior interviewer hear that a junior does not? Answer before reading on.
coding-interview-loop.reveal: They hear an unbacked claim wearing a number. '40%' with no baseline, no measurement method, and no rejected alternative is a story you memorized, not evidence you can defend. The gold version names the artifact ('load-test transcript in the packet'), the rejected option ('read-replica — violated our consistency constraint'), and the failure it could cause ('stale reads on the checkout path'). The number is the hook; the defensible claim is the artifact behind it.

# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet

## Role target
- Targeting: Backend engineer (payments-adjacent) — rewards correctness under load

## 1. Claim (the resume bullet)
- "Cut p99 order-confirmation latency 4s -> 0.9s under 3x peak load without adding data-loss risk."

## 2. Context & assumptions
- Checkout p99 was 4s vs a 1s SLO; assumed recompute-per-request was the cause (later verified)

## 3. Selected approach  ·  Rejected approach
- Selected: precompute + short-TTL cache on the read path, invalidate on write
- Rejected: read-replica reads -> violated the no-stale-reads-on-checkout constraint

## 4. Expected failure (the autopsy)
- Feared: stale price shown after a write; verified invalidation fires within 1 write-cycle

## 5. Verification method (the proof)
- Artifact link map: load-test transcript, invalidation unit test, before/after p99 dashboard

## 6. Reviewer objection + response
- Q: "How is this not a happy-path story?" -> A: point to the stale-read test that FAILS the naive version

## 7. Repair notes  ·  Capstone connection
- Repair: first bullet had no baseline; added the 4s->0.9s measurement. Reused in capstone packet.

Rejected approach is the tell: Naming what you rejected AND why (read-replica violated the no-stale-reads constraint) is what separates a senior walkthrough from a feature tour. Anyone can name what they built.

The failure autopsy: The specific production failure you feared and how you ruled it out. 'It might break' is a vibe; 'stale price after a write, verified invalidation fires within one write-cycle' is defensible.
Artifact link map = the proof: Every claim points to an inspectable artifact: a transcript, a test, a dashboard. This is the section a reviewer actually opens. No link map, no defense.
Objection response points to evidence: The answer to 'prove it is not happy-path' is never more words — it is 'here is the test that FAILS the naive version.' The evidence answers, not you.

debugging-interview.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'debugged it' if your story is a hero narrative with no evidence trail. 'I found the bug and fixed it' with no commit, no metric, no regression test is a technical walkthrough a recruiter cannot verify and an engineer will puncture in one follow-up.

debugging-interview.text: Second-round loop, senior engineer across the table: 'Tell me about a hard bug you debugged.' You launch into the story you tell friends — and forty seconds in they cut you off with 'wait, how did you know it was the cache and not the query?' The story that kills at parties has no evidence, and the room just watched it fold.

A debugging interview is not a test of whether you can code — it is a test of whether your judgment is inspectable under pressure. This lesson turns a real incident you lived into a role-targeted evidence packet: the same artifact your recruiter screen, technical walkthrough, and resume bullet all draw from.

debugging-interview.prompt: 'I noticed the app was slow, so I dug into the code and found a bug and fixed it, and it was much faster.' Before you polish that answer — what will an interviewer distrust about it? Answer before reading on.
debugging-interview.reveal: It is a highlight reel with the evidence edited out. 'Slow' is not a signal, 'dug into the code' is not a method, 'found a bug' skips the isolation, and 'much faster' is a vibe. A senior hears four unverifiable claims and one follow-up question ('how did you isolate it?') collapses the whole thing. The gold version leads with the exact failing signal — 'p99 checkout latency was 4s against a 1s SLO' — because a real signal is the one part of the story an interviewer can imagine seeing on a dashboard.

# Debugging Interview Defense Packet
## Role target: Backend / Platform SWE (mid)

## STAR answer (spoken, ~90s)
- S (Situation): Checkout p99 latency was 4s against a 1s SLO; conversions down ~6% since a Tuesday deploy.
- T (Task): Find the cause and cut p99 back under SLO without a daytime rollback of the release.
- A (Action): Ranked 3 causes; cheapest kill-test first -> gateway traces showed the slow span was our order-lookup, not the DB. Isolated to an N+1 introduced by the deploy (per-item price fetch in a loop).
- R (Result): Batched the fetch; p99 dropped 4s -> 0.7s; added a regression test asserting <=1 query per lookup.

## Artifact link map (claim -> evidence)
- '4s p99 / 1s SLO'        -> dashboard snapshot: grafana/checkout-latency?from=deploy
- 'slow span was our service' -> trace ID a1b9f in gateway logs (attached)
- 'N+1 from the deploy'     -> diff in commit 7c21e4 (loop introduced), fix in commit e0f83a
- 'held after fix'          -> test tests/test_order_lookup.py::test_no_n_plus_one (fails on 7c21e4)

## Resume bullet
- Cut checkout p99 latency 4s -> 0.7s by isolating a deploy-introduced N+1 via distributed tracing; added a query-count regression test to prevent recurrence.

## Objection response (scripted)
- Q: 'How do you know it was the N+1 and not just load easing off?'
- A: 'The regression test fails on the offending commit and passes on the fix, and the latency drop is stepwise at the deploy of e0f83a, not gradual. I can show both.'
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.

Role target first: Role targeting is a choice, not a default. The same incident is framed for the bar you are interviewing against — a platform role wants the tracing, a product role wants the conversion recovery.

STAR, but S leads with the signal: The Situation opens on a measured failing signal (4s vs 1s SLO), not 'it was slow'. That single number is the part of the story an interviewer can picture on a dashboard — it buys their trust for the rest.

The Action IS the isolation: Weak answers say 'I found it'. This names the kill-test order and the disqualifying evidence (gateway trace showed the slow span was ours, not the DB). Isolation is the seam the reviewer will probe — front-load it.

The artifact link map: This is the whole skill. Every claim in the STAR answer is bound to an inspectable artifact — a dashboard, a trace ID, a commit, a test. A claim with no row here is a claim you cannot defend.

The resume bullet is a projection of the packet: The bullet is the packet compressed: metric delta (4s -> 0.7s), method (distributed tracing), and durability (regression test). It survives a recruiter screen because the walkthrough behind it is real.

storyboard.say: It starts with a real incident you actually lived. On its own it's just a war story with no evidence a stranger could check.
Quantify it first: turn the incident into a measured failing signal, a number you saw, not an adjective you felt.
Route that signal into the isolation step, where you ruled causes out. This is the seam where hero stories break.
Isolation feeds the fix, then verification: you name what you changed and show the signal actually recovered.
Now link every claim to an artifact a stranger could open. That bundle becomes your defense packet.
The reviewer probes exactly the isolation seam: how did you know it was the cache and not the query? The packet must survive it.

# Debugging Interview Defense Packet
## Role target: Backend / Platform SWE (mid)

## STAR answer (spoken, ~90s)
- S (Situation): Checkout p99 latency was 4s against a 1s SLO; conversions down ~6% since a Tuesday deploy.
- T (Task): Find the cause and cut p99 back under SLO without a daytime rollback of the release.
- A (Action): Ranked 3 causes; cheapest kill-test first -> gateway traces showed the slow span was our order-lookup, not the DB. Isolated to an N+1 introduced by the deploy (per-item price fetch in a loop).
- R (Result): Batched the fetch; p99 dropped 4s -> 0.7s; added a regression test asserting <=1 query per lookup.

## Artifact link map (claim -> evidence)
- '4s p99 / 1s SLO'        -> dashboard snapshot: grafana/checkout-latency?from=deploy
- 'slow span was our service' -> trace ID a1b9f in gateway logs (attached)
- 'N+1 from the deploy'     -> diff in commit 7c21e4 (loop introduced), fix in commit e0f83a
- 'held after fix'          -> test tests/test_order_lookup.py::test_no_n_plus_one (fails on 7c21e4)

## Resume bullet
- Cut checkout p99 latency 4s -> 0.7s by isolating a deploy-introduced N+1 via distributed tracing; added a query-count regression test to prevent recurrence.

## Objection response (scripted)
- Q: 'How do you know it was the N+1 and not just load easing off?'
- A: 'The regression test fails on the offending commit and passes on the fix, and the latency drop is stepwise at the deploy of e0f83a, not gradual. I can show both.'

steps.label: Role target first
steps.note: Role targeting is a choice, not a default. The same incident is framed for the bar you are interviewing against — a platform role wants the tracing, a product role wants the conversion recovery.

steps.label: STAR, but S leads with the signal
steps.note: The Situation opens on a measured failing signal (4s vs 1s SLO), not 'it was slow'. That single number is the part of the story an interviewer can picture on a dashboard — it buys their trust for the rest.

steps.label: The Action IS the isolation
steps.note: Weak answers say 'I found it'. This names the kill-test order and the disqualifying evidence (gateway trace showed the slow span was ours, not the DB). Isolation is the seam the reviewer will probe — front-load it.

steps.label: The artifact link map
steps.note: This is the whole skill. Every claim in the STAR answer is bound to an inspectable artifact — a dashboard, a trace ID, a commit, a test. A claim with no row here is a claim you cannot defend.

steps.label: The resume bullet is a projection of the packet
steps.note: The bullet is the packet compressed: metric delta (4s -> 0.7s), method (distributed tracing), and durability (regression test). It survives a recruiter screen because the walkthrough behind it is real.

steps.label: The objection response, pre-scripted

debugging-interview.text: The senior tell in a debugging interview is not the size of the bug — it is whether your story has a falsifiable proof. Junior candidates prove the fix by asserting it worked; senior candidates point to the regression test that fails on the offending commit and passes on the fix. SWEBOK treats verification and validation (Software Testing, Software Quality) as core knowledge areas of the discipline: sound work is backed by verification, not narrative. (Reframe from 'an engineer's claims' to 'the work/software,' which is what SWEBOK actually addresses, and drop the unverified ABET co-attribution.) In the room, 'here is the test that would catch it again' beats 'trust me, it was faster.'

debugging-interview.question: A reviewer says: 'Point me to the exact evidence that proves this is not just a happy-path answer.' Which response actually satisfies the challenge?
options: 'I'm very confident it was the N+1 — I've seen this pattern many times.'
'The regression test fails on the commit that introduced the bug and passes on the fix, and the latency drop is stepwise at that deploy — I can show you both.'
'The whole team agreed it was the right fix and we shipped it.'
'The app was noticeably faster afterward and the complaints stopped.'
debugging-interview.explanation: Only option 2 points to a falsifiable artifact: a test that discriminates the bad commit from the fix, plus a stepwise metric change tied to the deploy. Confidence (1), consensus (3), and a vibe (4) are all unverifiable — exactly the happy-path adjectives the reviewer challenge exists to expose. The artifact link map is what turns 'trust me' into 'open this.'

# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet
## Claim (the resume bullet)
- Cut notification p95 from 900ms to 140ms under 5x burst by moving to an async queue
## Context & constraint
- Constraint (non-negotiable): at-least-once delivery, p95 < 200ms at peak
## Selected approach
- Async queue (SQS) + idempotent consumer; dedup on message id
## Rejected approach (and why)
- Synchronous retries in-request: simpler, but blows the 200ms budget on burst
## Expected failure (what I feared)
- Duplicate sends on redelivery -> user gets 2 texts; mitigated by idempotency key
## Verification method
- Load test at 5x peak: 0 dropped events, p95 = 140ms, 0 duplicate deliveries
## Reviewer objection + answer
- "Why not Kafka?" -> no replay/ordering need; SQS is cheaper to run solo
## Repair notes / capstone connection
- Feeds capstone: same packet becomes the system-design walkthrough story
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.
The claim (resume bullet): One line, quantified, no adjective doing the work of a number. 'Improved reliability' is banned; 'p95 900ms -> 140ms under 5x burst' is a claim a reviewer can attack.

The hard constraint: The non-negotiable that must rule out at least one plausible option — here, the 200ms budget is what kills synchronous retries. A constraint that eliminates nothing is decoration.
Selected approach: Name it specifically (SQS + idempotent consumer), not 'a queue'. The specificity is what survives a technical walkthrough.

Rejected approach — the load-bearing section: This is the evidence of a real tradeoff. A credible option (sync retries), and the reason it lost (the constraint). If you can't fill this honestly, you did not make the call.
Expected failure + mitigation: The failure autopsy: name what 'wrong' looks like in production (duplicate texts) and how you defused it. This is what separates a maker from a name-dropper.
Verification method: The proof. A number from a test, not a claim from memory: 0 dropped, p95 140ms, 0 duplicates. No proof caps the claim's credibility.
Reviewer objection + answer: Pre-load the hostile follow-up ('why not Kafka?') and answer it with the constraint, not a shrug. This is the on-site question, rehearsed.
Capstone connection: The same packet is reused as the capstone system-design story. If it can't be reused, it isn't premium-ready.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

storyboard.say: Every claim on your resume starts here: a real tradeoff you actually made under a hard constraint.
The right move is to capture that decision into a defense packet — the artifact a reviewer can inspect.
The packet grounds your portfolio claim, so the resume bullet is backed by evidence, not just words.
Grounded that way, the claim survives the screen and holds up as an interview defense on-site.
Now the failure path: skip the packet and you carry only a bare claim with no rejected option, no proof.
One hostile question — 'what did you almost choose instead?' — and the bare claim collapses under follow-up.
The repair routes the collapse back to the packet: write the road-not-taken, the option you rejected and why.
The invariant: your evidence is the rejected alternative. No defensible road-not-taken means the decision wasn't yours.

# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet
## Claim (the resume bullet)
- Cut notification p95 from 900ms to 140ms under 5x burst by moving to an async queue
## Context & constraint
- Constraint (non-negotiable): at-least-once delivery, p95 < 200ms at peak
## Selected approach
- Async queue (SQS) + idempotent consumer; dedup on message id
## Rejected approach (and why)
- Synchronous retries in-request: simpler, but blows the 200ms budget on burst
## Expected failure (what I feared)
- Duplicate sends on redelivery -> user gets 2 texts; mitigated by idempotency key
## Verification method
- Load test at 5x peak: 0 dropped events, p95 = 140ms, 0 duplicate deliveries
## Reviewer objection + answer
- "Why not Kafka?" -> no replay/ordering need; SQS is cheaper to run solo
## Repair notes / capstone connection
- Feeds capstone: same packet becomes the system-design walkthrough story

steps.label: The claim (resume bullet)
steps.note: One line, quantified, no adjective doing the work of a number. 'Improved reliability' is banned; 'p95 900ms -> 140ms under 5x burst' is a claim a reviewer can attack.

steps.label: The hard constraint
steps.note: The non-negotiable that must rule out at least one plausible option — here, the 200ms budget is what kills synchronous retries. A constraint that eliminates nothing is decoration.

steps.label: Selected approach
steps.note: Name it specifically (SQS + idempotent consumer), not 'a queue'. The specificity is what survives a technical walkthrough.

steps.label: Rejected approach — the load-bearing section
steps.note: This is the evidence of a real tradeoff. A credible option (sync retries), and the reason it lost (the constraint). If you can't fill this honestly, you did not make the call.

steps.label: Expected failure + mitigation
steps.note: The failure autopsy: name what 'wrong' looks like in production (duplicate texts) and how you defused it. This is what separates a maker from a name-dropper.

steps.label: Verification method
steps.note: The proof. A number from a test, not a claim from memory: 0 dropped, p95 140ms, 0 duplicates. No proof caps the claim's credibility.

steps.label: Reviewer objection + answer
steps.note: Pre-load the hostile follow-up ('why not Kafka?') and answer it with the constraint, not a shrug. This is the on-site question, rehearsed.

steps.label: Capstone connection
steps.note: The same packet is reused as the capstone system-design story. If it can't be reused, it isn't premium-ready.

architecture-tradeoffs.text: The senior tell in a system-design interview is not naming the right technology — it's naming the constraint that made the choice non-arbitrary, then volunteering the option you rejected before being asked. SWEBOK frames architecture as tradeoff analysis under quality-attribute constraints, not component selection. If your story only defends what you shipped, you're describing a decision; if it can defend why you didn't ship the alternative, you're demonstrating judgment.

architecture-tradeoffs.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Point to the exact evidence that this is a real tradeoff you owned, not a happy-path answer.' Which response passes?
options: "I chose a message queue because it's the industry-standard pattern for decoupling services."

"Here's the packet: the constraint was p95 < 200ms at at-least-once delivery, I rejected synchronous retries because they'd blow that budget under burst, and the load test shows 0 dropped events with p95 at 140ms."
"Everyone on the team agreed it was the best choice, and it's been running in production for a year."
"I read three blog posts and a Kafka-vs-SQS comparison before deciding."
architecture-tradeoffs.explanation: Only option 2 points at inspectable evidence: a hard constraint, a named rejected option with the reason it lost, and a proof with numbers. 'Industry-standard' (1) is an appeal to authority with no constraint; 'the team agreed' / 'running a year' (3) is social proof, not a tradeoff; 'I read blog posts' (4) is input, not a defended decision. The reviewer challenge is answered only by the rejected-option-plus-proof, which is exactly what the packet forces you to write down.

ai-tooling-interview.proof: The AI-tooling section of portfolio_story_and_interview_defense_packet.md: a portfolio claim that names YOUR decision (not the tool's output), a resume bullet with a verified outcome, a STAR walkthrough, and a scripted answer to 'so the AI wrote it?'. A peer reviewer reads it and can tell what you decided that the tool could not.
ai-tooling-interview.unlock: Your packet names the judgment you supplied on top of the tool, backs every claim with an artifact link, and has a defense answer for the 'did you actually build this?' objection.
ai-tooling-interview.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'used AI tooling' if your evidence is just 'I prompted Copilot and it worked.' That is a tool operating, not an engineer deciding. The claim must name what you accepted, rejected, verified, or corrected in the model's output — the part a reviewer can only get from you.

ai-tooling-interview.text: Final-round panel. You describe the feature you shipped, and the staff engineer leans in: 'Cool — but the AI wrote most of that, right? What did YOU actually do?' Every candidate who treated the tool as the accomplishment dies on that sentence. The one who framed the tool as an instrument they steered gets the offer.

AI tooling is now assumed, not impressive — so the interview signal has inverted: reviewers no longer ask 'can you use it' but 'can you be trusted to judge its output.' This lesson turns your AI-assisted work into an evidence packet that survives a recruiter screen and a technical walkthrough by foregrounding your judgment, not the tool's.

- Role target: backend/full-stack roles that value AI-augmented velocity + code review rigor
- Context: shipped an internal payments dashboard solo in 5 days; team norm was ~2 weeks
- Resume bullet: "Shipped a payments dashboard in 5 days using AI-drafted scaffolding; caught and rewrote an N+1 aggregation the model generated, cutting p95 900ms -> 120ms."
- What the tool did: drafted the CRUD layer, React table, and a first-pass SQL aggregation
- What I decided (attribution): rejected the model's per-row query, replaced with a single grouped aggregation; added the index the model omitted; wrote the tests it did not
- Verification: load test 900ms -> 120ms p95 (link: /artifacts/loadtest.png); 41 tests, 87% cov
- Rejected approach: accepting the AI output as-is (would have shipped the N+1 to prod)
- Objection response: "The AI drafted; I owned correctness. Here is the query it wrote and the one I shipped."

steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.
Role targeting: Name the role this story is FOR. The same project sells differently to a velocity-focused startup vs a rigor-focused fintech — target it.
The resume bullet: One line that survives a 6-second recruiter screen: outcome + your correction + a verified number. The tool is the instrument, the fix is yours.
Tool did vs I decided: The two-line split IS the skill. If the 'I decided' line is empty, you have no interview story — you have a tool demo.
Verification with an artifact link: Every number links to proof (load test, coverage). 'The AI made it faster' is a vibe; '900ms -> 120ms, here is the graph' is evidence.
The rejected approach: Naming what you did NOT do — accept the raw output — is the clearest signal of judgment on the panel.
The objection response, scripted: Pre-write the answer to 'so the AI did it?'. Point to the query it wrote and the one you shipped. This line wins the round.

storyboard.say: Everything starts here: one AI-assisted project. The only variable is how you frame it — the same work can be an asset or a liability.
Frame the tool as the accomplishment and you build a tool-worship claim — 'the AI did this' — which routes straight to rejection.
Frame it as judgment instead — what you decided on top of the model — and the project becomes a portfolio claim you can defend.
That claim becomes a resume bullet that clears the recruiter screen, because AI use is now assumed, not impressive.
The screen passes you to round two: the technical walkthrough, where a staff engineer asks what YOU actually did.
Here the paths converge. Fail to attribute your decisions and even a judgment-framed claim gets cut on that one sentence.
Name what you accepted, rejected, verified, and corrected — that attribution earns trust and the offer.
The invariant is attribution: judgment over output is the proof, and tool-worship is the only real failure mode.

cloud-data-interview.text: The recruiter screen went fine, so now a staff data engineer is across the table: 'You said you built a pipeline on the cloud. What actually broke, and how did you know it was fixed?' The candidate who rehearsed a paragraph freezes; the one who built a defense packet turns their laptop around and points at the exact evidence.

A cloud-data interview is not a memory test — it is a proof exchange: they probe a claim, you produce an artifact. This packet is the reusable evidence unit you carry into role targeting, the recruiter screen, the technical walkthrough, and later the whole career-readiness portfolio.

cloud-data-interview.prompt: An interviewer asks about your project and you answer: 'I built a scalable, real-time data pipeline on AWS using best practices.' Before reading on — what is wrong with that as an answer?
cloud-data-interview.reveal: It is a brochure, not evidence. 'Scalable', 'real-time', and 'best practices' are claims the interviewer can neither verify nor probe — so the good ones stop trusting you and the great ones ask 'scalable to what? proven how?' and watch you scramble. The gold version front-loads the artifact: 'p95 ingest latency was 40 min, the SLA was 5; here's the trace showing the batch-window bottleneck, and here's the query that proved the fix held.' Adjectives repel probing; artifacts invite it — and inviting it is the whole signal.

# Interview Defense Packet — Cloud Data Pipeline

## Role target
- Target: Data Engineer (batch → streaming), mid-level, AWS shop
- The bar this hits: owns an ingest pipeline end-to-end + can prove a fix

## STAR story
- Situation: nightly S3 → Redshift load, p95 ingest 40 min, SLA 5 min
- Task: cut latency without a full re-architecture (2-week window)
- Action: traced the batch window; replaced one 40-min full-table swap
  with CDC micro-batches on the changed partitions
- Result: p95 ingest 40 min → 4 min; SLA met 29/30 nights

## Evidence artifacts (inspectable)
- architecture.png — S3 → Lambda → staging → Redshift, CDC edge marked
- proof.sql — query comparing max(loaded_at) vs max(source_ts) per run
- run_metrics.csv — 30-night before/after p95 latency

## Selected vs rejected approach
- Selected: CDC micro-batch on changed partitions (incremental, reversible)
- Rejected: full Redshift re-cluster + Spark rewrite (6-week, one-way door)

## Expected failure + verification
- Feared failure: silent partial loads (rows missing, no error)
- Verification: proof.sql row-count reconciliation source vs target, per run

## Reviewer objection + repair
- Objection: 'was 4 min just an easy night?' → run_metrics.csv shows 30 nights
- Repair note: added a nightly reconciliation alert (was manual)

## Capstone connection
- Reused as the 'systems I've shipped' exhibit in the portfolio capstone
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.

Role target first: Name the exact role and the bar. A packet aimed at 'Data Engineer, AWS, owns ingest' reads completely differently from one aimed at 'Analytics Engineer' — role targeting decides which claims matter.

STAR with numbers, not adjectives: Situation and Result carry the metric (40 min → 4 min, SLA 29/30). 'Scalable' never appears; the number does the persuading. This is the interview story a recruiter screen can repeat back.
Every claim gets an artifact: The claim 'I cut latency' is worthless until it points at proof.sql and run_metrics.csv. This is the evidence packet — the thing you turn your laptop around to show.

Name the rejected option: Selected (CDC micro-batch, reversible) vs rejected (full rewrite, one-way door). Naming what you chose AGAINST is the single strongest signal of judgment in a technical walkthrough.
The feared failure + how you'd catch it: Silent partial loads is the realistic production failure. Verification (row-count reconciliation) is the proof that separates 'it ran' from 'it was correct'.

Pre-load the objection: 'Was 4 min just an easy night?' is the reviewer challenge. Answering it in the packet (30-night data + a reconciliation alert repair) means the hard question becomes a chance to show more evidence.
Wire it to the capstone: If the packet can't be reused as a portfolio exhibit, it isn't premium-ready. This line is the bridge from one interview answer to the career-readiness portfolio.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

cloud-data-interview.subtitle: A project claim only earns trust when it routes to an artifact, a rejected option, and a proof. The dashed path is the failure mode: a claim with no evidence behind it collapses the moment it's probed.

nodes.description: 'show me it wasn't the happy path'

legend.label: adjective-only — no evidence to stand on

storyboard.say: It starts with a portfolio claim: 'I built a data pipeline on the cloud.' On its own, that sentence earns nothing yet.
You frame the claim as a STAR story so the reviewer hears the situation, the task, and the concrete action you took.
But a story needs receipts. The STAR points at an inspectable artifact: a diagram, a query, a test result, a dashboard.
The claim also defends via a rejected option, showing the tradeoff you weighed and why you chose this path over the alternative.
The artifact is verified by a proof: the test passed, the row counts matched, the run is reproducible on demand.
Now the proof answers the reviewer's objection head-on: 'what broke, and how did you know it was fixed?' You show, not tell.
The dashed failure mode: an adjective-only answer feeds a claim that collapses under probing, because nothing inspectable sits behind it.
The invariant: if a reviewer can't inspect the proof, it isn't a portfolio claim, it's marketing. Carry the packet, not a paragraph.
