# Interview Defense Packet — Cloud Data Pipeline

## Role target
- Target: Data Engineer (batch → streaming), mid-level, AWS shop
- The bar this hits: owns an ingest pipeline end-to-end + can prove a fix

## STAR story
- Situation: nightly S3 → Redshift load, p95 ingest 40 min, SLA 5 min
- Task: cut latency without a full re-architecture (2-week window)
- Action: traced the batch window; replaced one 40-min full-table swap
  with CDC micro-batches on the changed partitions
- Result: p95 ingest 40 min → 4 min; SLA met 29/30 nights

## Evidence artifacts (inspectable)
- architecture.png — S3 → Lambda → staging → Redshift, CDC edge marked
- proof.sql — query comparing max(loaded_at) vs max(source_ts) per run
- run_metrics.csv — 30-night before/after p95 latency

## Selected vs rejected approach
- Selected: CDC micro-batch on changed partitions (incremental, reversible)
- Rejected: full Redshift re-cluster + Spark rewrite (6-week, one-way door)

## Expected failure + verification
- Feared failure: silent partial loads (rows missing, no error)
- Verification: proof.sql row-count reconciliation source vs target, per run

## Reviewer objection + repair
- Objection: 'was 4 min just an easy night?' → run_metrics.csv shows 30 nights
- Repair note: added a nightly reconciliation alert (was manual)

## Capstone connection
- Reused as the 'systems I've shipped' exhibit in the portfolio capstone

steps.label: Role target first
steps.note: Name the exact role and the bar. A packet aimed at 'Data Engineer, AWS, owns ingest' reads completely differently from one aimed at 'Analytics Engineer' — role targeting decides which claims matter.

steps.label: STAR with numbers, not adjectives
steps.note: Situation and Result carry the metric (40 min → 4 min, SLA 29/30). 'Scalable' never appears; the number does the persuading. This is the interview story a recruiter screen can repeat back.

steps.label: Every claim gets an artifact
steps.note: The claim 'I cut latency' is worthless until it points at proof.sql and run_metrics.csv. This is the evidence packet — the thing you turn your laptop around to show.

steps.label: Name the rejected option
steps.note: Selected (CDC micro-batch, reversible) vs rejected (full rewrite, one-way door). Naming what you chose AGAINST is the single strongest signal of judgment in a technical walkthrough.

steps.label: The feared failure + how you'd catch it
steps.note: Silent partial loads is the realistic production failure. Verification (row-count reconciliation) is the proof that separates 'it ran' from 'it was correct'.

steps.label: Pre-load the objection
steps.note: 'Was 4 min just an easy night?' is the reviewer challenge. Answering it in the packet (30-night data + a reconciliation alert repair) means the hard question becomes a chance to show more evidence.

steps.label: Wire it to the capstone
steps.note: If the packet can't be reused as a portfolio exhibit, it isn't premium-ready. This line is the bridge from one interview answer to the career-readiness portfolio.

cloud-data-interview.text: SWEBOK centers evidence and verification, not vocabulary — and interviewers do the same instinctively. (Replace 'grade engineers on' with 'center'; SWEBOK describes the discipline, it does not grade individuals, and drop the unverified ABET co-attribution.) The senior-vs-junior tell: a strong candidate volunteers the artifact and the rejected option before being asked, because they know the interviewer's real question is never 'do you know the words' — it's 'can you prove the claim and defend the tradeoff.' Rehearse the proof, not the paragraph.

cloud-data-interview.question: A reviewer challenges you: 'Point to the exact evidence that proves this was more than a happy-path demo.' Which response earns trust?
options: 'I followed AWS best practices and it was very scalable, so it would definitely hold up.'

'Here is run_metrics.csv with 30 nights of before/after p95 latency, and proof.sql, the row-count reconciliation that catches silent partial loads — it flagged one bad night, which is how I found the missing partition.'
'I'm confident it worked because the demo ran fine when I showed my team.'
'The architecture was industry-standard, so failures were unlikely.'
cloud-data-interview.explanation: Only option 2 points at inspectable artifacts (30-night metrics + a reconciliation query) AND names a real caught failure — proving the packet survives probing, not just the demo. The others substitute adjectives ('best practices', 'industry-standard') or a single unverified run for evidence, which is exactly the happy-path answer the reviewer is hunting for.

cloud-data-interview.intro: Prove your packet is evidence, not a brochure — no vibes:
items: Read your STAR Result aloud. If it contains an adjective ('scalable', 'robust') instead of a number or a checkable outcome, replace it with the metric.
For every claim, name the exact artifact a reviewer would open to verify it. If any claim has no artifact, it is marketing — cut it or produce the artifact.
Confirm you named a rejected approach and can say why you chose against it — a packet with only the chosen path hides your judgment.
State the feared failure (the realistic production one, e.g. silent partial loads) and the verification that would catch it. 'It ran' is not 'it was correct'.
Hand the packet to a peer: they should restate your project and point to the one artifact that proves the fix held, with you silent.
Confirm the packet is reusable as a capstone/portfolio exhibit unchanged in structure — if it can't be reused, it isn't premium-ready.

State the reviewer objection you most fear on this project, and the exact evidence in your packet that answers it.

take-home-execution.text: The take-home passed the automated tests, so you relax — then the technical walkthrough opens with 'walk me through why you built it this way, and show me it actually works.' The candidate who wrote a defense packet points to a link map and a failure autopsy; the one who only shipped code freezes, because they proved the happy path and nothing else.

A take-home is not graded on 'it runs' — it is graded on whether a reviewer can trust your judgment under questioning. This lesson turns raw project evidence into a role-targeted, defensible packet: the same artifact your recruiter screen, technical walkthrough, and capstone all reuse.

take-home-execution.prompt: Your take-home submission passes every provided test. A strong reviewer is now MORE likely to probe one specific thing. What — and why? Answer before reading on.
take-home-execution.reveal: They probe what your tests do NOT cover — the failure case. Passing tests only prove the paths you thought of; a senior reviewer assumes a happy-path solution and pushes on the edges, the tradeoff you rejected, and 'what breaks in production?' The packet that survives names its own weakest point BEFORE the interviewer does. Volunteering the failure autopsy reads as judgment; getting caught without one reads as a guess that happened to compile.

# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet — take-home: rate-limited URL shortener

## Context & assumptions
- Task: shorten URLs, 1k req/s target, single region assumed (not stated → I chose it)

## Selected vs rejected approach
- Selected: in-memory token bucket per key, Redis for the counter (survives restart)
- Rejected: DB row-per-request (rejected: write amplification kills the 1k/s target)

## Expected failure (the path my tests do NOT cover)
- Redis unreachable mid-request → limiter fails OPEN, floods origin. Autopsy below.

## Verification method
- k6 load test at 1.2k req/s → 429s appear at the cap; artifact: load/k6-report.html

## Claim → evidence map (role targeting: backend, reliability)
- Claim "handles 1k req/s"            → evidence: load/k6-report.html (p99 42ms)
- Claim "limiter is correct"          → evidence: test/limiter_boundary_test.py (edge cases)
- Claim "degrades safely"             → evidence: test/redis_down_test.py + the repair below

## STAR interview story
- S/T: take-home wanted a limiter at 1k/s. A: token bucket + Redis counter.
  R: 1.2k/s sustained, but I found it fails-open when Redis dies — so I fixed it.

## Resume bullet
- Built a token-bucket rate limiter (1.2k req/s, p99 42ms) with a fail-CLOSED
  Redis-outage path, verified by k6 load + fault-injection tests.

## Reviewer objection + response
- Objection: "Your tests all pass — what breaks in prod?"
- Response: Redis outage failed open (autopsy); repaired to fail closed; test proves it.

## Repair note (reusable rule)
- Before shipping any limiter: write the dependency-down test FIRST; default to fail-closed.

## Capstone connection
- This packet drops into the career readiness packet as the backend proof entry.
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.
Context & assumptions: Name the assumption the prompt left unstated (single region). Reviewers probe unstated assumptions first — surfacing yours reads as judgment, not luck.
Selected vs rejected approach: The rejected option with a reason is the tell. Anyone can name what they built; a senior candidate names what they DIDN'T and why the constraint killed it.
Expected failure: State the path your tests do NOT cover before the interviewer finds it. Volunteering your weakest point is the single strongest move in a walkthrough.
Verification method: A named, inspectable proof (k6-report.html) — not 'I tested it'. Proof the reviewer can open beats a claim they must trust.
The claim → evidence map: The core artifact. Each portfolio claim links to a file a reviewer opens in seconds. An unlinked claim is a vibe — cut it or link it.
STAR story + resume bullet: Same evidence, three surfaces: the STAR story for behavioral rounds, the bullet for the recruiter screen. The result line names the FIX you found, not just the pass.
Objection, repair, capstone: The reviewer challenge answered in advance, a repair that is a reusable rule ('dependency-down test first'), and the hook that lets the capstone reuse this exact packet.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

storyboard.say: It starts with your take-home submission. But the raw submission isn't the deliverable — it's only the raw material for what you actually defend.
First, extract the portfolio claims: every assertion your project makes about your judgment, your design, and your results.
Now attach evidence. The claim-to-evidence map binds each claim to the exact inspectable artifact that proves it — an unlinked claim is just a vibe.
Recruiter-screen fluff — the unlinked claim with nothing behind it — must never pass through the map into the technical walkthrough.
With claims linked, probe the gaps. The failure autopsy is the decision point: does each claim survive hard questioning, or does it break?
When a claim fails, the answer is 'no' — you don't hide it. You write a repair note: the failure you expected and how you verified the fix.
Two paths reach the walkthrough: the link map traces every claim to evidence, and the repair note defends the ones that once broke.
The invariant: every claim is traceable to inspectable evidence. That's the packet that survives 'walk me through why you built it this way.'

- Redis unreachable mid-request → limiter fails OPEN, floods origin. Autopsy below.

## Verification method
- k6 load test at 1.2k req/s → 429s appear at the cap; artifact: load/k6-report.html

## Claim → evidence map (role targeting: backend, reliability)
- Claim "handles 1k req/s"            → evidence: load/k6-report.html (p99 42ms)
- Claim "limiter is correct"          → evidence: test/limiter_boundary_test.py (edge cases)
- Claim "degrades safely"             → evidence: test/redis_down_test.py + the repair below

## STAR interview story
- S/T: take-home wanted a limiter at 1k/s. A: token bucket + Redis counter.
  R: 1.2k/s sustained, but I found it fails-open when Redis dies — so I fixed it.

## Resume bullet
- Built a token-bucket rate limiter (1.2k req/s, p99 42ms) with a fail-CLOSED
  Redis-outage path, verified by k6 load + fault-injection tests.

## Reviewer objection + response
- Objection: "Your tests all pass — what breaks in prod?"
- Response: Redis outage failed open (autopsy); repaired to fail closed; test proves it.

## Repair note (reusable rule)
- Before shipping any limiter: write the dependency-down test FIRST; default to fail-closed.

## Capstone connection
- This packet drops into the career readiness packet as the backend proof entry.

outreach-networking.text: Two engineers apply to the same role. One drops a resume into the portal and waits with 400 others; the other messages the hiring manager with one line — 'I rebuilt a checkout that was losing 4% at p99, here's the memo' — and a link. Guess who gets the reply. The gap is not talent. It is that one of them carried proof to a named person, and the other shouted into a portal.

This is the synthesis lesson: every artifact you built across the course — the memo, the story bank, the resume bullet — only converts into a job when it reaches the right person with the proof attached. Outreach is the delivery layer for your evidence packet, and networking is how the proof travels before you ever hit 'apply'.

It asks them to figure out who you are, what you can do, and what you want — three jobs, no evidence, from a stranger. The fix is not warmer wording; it is a payload: one named portfolio claim tied to an artifact, one role you are targeting, one ask they can grant in ten seconds. 'Looking for opportunities' is the tell of someone with nothing to show — you replace it with something to show.

# Writing the Outreach section, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Turn one warm-lead or cold outreach you actually need to send into the Outreach section of portfolio_story_and_interview_defense_packet.md: the role you are targeting, the specific person, the one portfolio claim you lead with, the proof link you attach, and the single ask — so a recruiter screen becomes a conversation, not a void.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only best_pure at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Name the target and the role. If the 'to' field is a team, a portal, or 'whoever's hiring,' it is a spray, not outreach — fix it.
# 2. Read your portfolio claim aloud. If it names a topic ('worked on performance') instead of a proof ('4.1s->0.9s, memo linked'), it will get ghosted — attach the number and the artifact.
# 3. Confirm the artifact link is actually in the message and actually opens to your evidence, not a bare profile.
# 4. Count the asks. Exactly one, grantable in ten seconds. Zero asks and two asks both kill the reply.
# 5. Confirm the claim maps to a resume bullet AND a STAR answer you can walk through — because a reply of 'tell me more' turns this into your first technical walkthrough.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

CHANNELS = [
    ("portal-application", 0.02, 5),
    ("cold-outreach-with-proof", 0.12, 25),
    ("warm-intro", 0.35, 90),
]
BUDGET = 600


def pure(channel, budget):
    name, rate, minutes = channel
    sends = budget // minutes
    expected = round(sends * rate, 2)
    return sends, expected


def best_pure(channels, budget):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied career fixtures.
    # Return inspectable evidence; do not invent experience, outcomes, or market data.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

def mixed(channels, budget, split):
    total = 0.0
    for ch in channels:
        minutes = int(budget * split[ch[0]])
        total += (minutes // ch[2]) * ch[1]
    return round(total, 2)


for ch in CHANNELS:
    sends, expected = pure(ch, BUDGET)
    print(f"{ch[0]}: {sends} sends -> {expected} expected conversations")
print(f"best pure strategy: {best_pure(CHANNELS, BUDGET)}")
split = {"portal-application": 0.2, "cold-outreach-with-proof": 0.5,
         "warm-intro": 0.3}
print(f"20/50/30 mix: {mixed(CHANNELS, BUDGET, split)} expected conversations")

storyboard.say: Every artifact you built — the memo, the number, the link — starts as one evidence packet waiting to travel.
You pull one claim and its link out of the packet and turn it into a draft message aimed at a named person.
Before you send, one decision gates everything: is the proof actually attached to this message?
Say no — no proof — and you default to portal spray, dropping a resume in with four hundred others.
That path dead-ends in silence. Noise with your name on it gets ghosted every time.
The repair edge is the whole skill: go back, attach the artifact, and re-enter the flow with proof in hand.
Say yes — proof travels — and the message clears the recruiter screen instead of the spam pile.
The claim holds under scrutiny, so you get the reply and the intro. Evidence traveling with the message is the invariant.

application-pipeline.text: Two engineers submit for the same role. One writes "passionate about building scalable systems"; the recruiter's eyes glaze at bullet three. The other writes "cut p95 checkout latency 4.1s → 900ms; walkthrough + load-test transcript on request" — and the recruiter clicks the link before finishing the page.

This is the synthesis lesson of the course: role targeting, proof rewriting, resumes, profiles, STAR stories, and the technical walkthrough stop being separate exercises and become one pipeline. # Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet

## Target role
Backend / Platform Engineer — high-throughput services

## Portfolio claim (names the proof, not the topic)
Cut p95 order-confirmation latency 4.1s -> 0.9s under 2x peak load.
  -> artifact: /proof/loadtest_before_after.md + PR #482 (worker backfill)

## Resume bullet (recruiter-screen version)
Reduced p95 checkout latency 78% (4.1s->0.9s) by fixing a lagging
  index worker; verified with a k6 load test at 2x peak.

## STAR story (behavioral defense)
S: checkout p95 breached the 1s SLO during a promo.
T: restore SLO without daytime downtime (hard constraint).
A: framed it as index lag, ranked 3 hypotheses, killed 2 cheaply,
   shipped worker fix + off-hours backfill.
R: 4.1s->0.9s p95; zero data loss; SLO held next promo.

## Selected vs rejected approach
Selected: fix worker + backfill (reversible, no downtime).
Rejected: full reindex — violates no-daytime-downtime constraint.

## Expected failure (the autopsy I can defend)
Backfill could miss events silently; guard = dead-letter count == 0.

## Reviewer objection + response
Q: "Did you cause the lag?"  A: no — gateway logs show 500s never
  reached my service; timestamp compare isolated the worker.

## Capstone connection
Reused as the flagship story in the career-readiness packet.

The failure autopsy: You name the way it could have broken and the guard that caught it. Reviewers trust the candidate who volunteers the failure mode.
The objection is pre-scripted: Answer the hostile question before it is asked, with evidence (gateway logs), not adjectives.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

# Building the packet, one section at a time
#
# Mission: Take one project you actually shipped and convert it into a role-targeted Application Pipeline: a portfolio claim wired to a named artifact, a STAR interview story, a recruiter-screen resume bullet, and a scripted answer to the one objection a reviewer will raise — all in a single defensible packet.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only diagnose at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Every portfolio claim names a specific artifact you could open in under five seconds (a path, a PR, a transcript). If any claim has no link, it is a slogan — cut or back it.
# 2. The resume bullet contains a number and a mechanism, and survives a 7-second read: a peer skims it and can restate what you did and how you proved it.
# 3. The STAR Result restates the exact same metric as the portfolio claim — screen and interview must never contradict each other.
# 4. You named one rejected approach AND the constraint that ruled it out. If you can't, you have described work, not a decision.
# 5. You wrote the one hostile objection a reviewer will raise, and a response that points to evidence (a log, a metric, a test), not to an adjective.
# 6. The packet is aimed at a named role — the same project would be framed differently for a different target, and you can say how.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

    screens = math.ceil(onsites / bench[1])
    applies = math.ceil(screens / bench[0])
    per_week = math.ceil(applies / weeks)
    return applies, screens, onsites, per_week


def diagnose(actual, bench):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied career fixtures.
    # Return inspectable evidence; do not invent experience, outcomes, or market data.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

applies, screens, onsites, per_week = plan(2, BENCH, 8)
print(f"to get 2 offers: {applies} applies -> {screens} screens -> {onsites} onsites")
print(f"weekly quota: {per_week} targeted applications")
for stage, actual_rate, bench_rate, verdict in diagnose(ACTUAL, BENCH):
    print(f"{stage}: {actual_rate} vs {bench_rate} benchmark — {verdict}")

storyboard.say: It starts with something real: a shipped project. Not a wish, an artifact you actually built and can open.
Distill that project into one evidence packet — the specific artifact plus the metric that proves it moved.
The packet targets the role as a resume bullet, then faces the recruiter screen — a brutal seven-second test.
Here's the failure mode: an unbacked claim hits that same screen with no link, and the recruiter's answer is just no.
But a backed claim earns a maybe, which pulls you into a STAR story — situation, task, action, result.
Then prove it: the STAR story opens into a technical walkthrough where you defend the work at the whiteboard.
The loop closes — the walkthrough points back to the same packet. One artifact carried every stage, evidence never lost.
The invariant: a claim you cannot open is a claim you cannot defend. Every bullet names an inspectable artifact.

offer-negotiation.text: The offer lands: $145k, and the recruiter says "we think this is really competitive." You have four hours of interview evidence proving you clear the bar — and if you say "sounds good, thank you" you leave $20k a year on the table for the length of the job, because you never turned that proof into a number.

This is the synthesis lesson of the Interview Career track: every prior move — the portfolio claim, the interview story, the technical walkthrough — was building the evidence packet you now spend at the table. Negotiation is where proof becomes compensation, or where it quietly evaporates.

offer-negotiation.reveal: Do not name a number first — anchor to evidence, then defer. # Writing the negotiation section, one line at a time

# Mission: Take one real (or realistic) offer you could plausibly receive and write the negotiation section of portfolio_story_and_interview_defense_packet.md: the target number backed by market evidence, your one non-negotiable constraint, the counter script, and the exact concession you would accept in trade — all tied to proof, not vibes.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only value_offer at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Your target number has a named source (Levels.fyi / Glassdoor / recruiter intel) and a level, not 'the market.' If you cannot cite it, it is a guess — go find the anchor.

# 3. Your walk-away constraint (BATNA) is a concrete number or situation you would actually take, not 'a really good reason.' If it does not exist, the deadline will decide for you.
# 4. You brought at least one concession to trade — a non-comp lever you can give — so your counter is a deal, not a demand.
# 5. The counter script is written verbatim and reads as something you could say out loud, warm, in ten seconds, without improvising.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

OFFER_B = ("startup", 165_000, 0.0, 200_000, False)

    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

def raise_value(base_bump, bonus_pct, years=4):
    return int(years * (base_bump + base_bump * bonus_pct))


for offer in (OFFER_A, OFFER_B):

storyboard.say: The initial offer lands. It looks fine on its face, but 'fine' is not the test. You compare it against your evidence anchor.
The anchor is a market range you can actually cite. It sets your target and the one constraint you will not cross.
That target drives the counter. Every ask is backed by proof and paired with a concession you would trade.
The counter is the decision point. From here the loop resolves one of two ways.
If the gap closes, you trade your concession for the number and accept. Proof became compensation.
If it lands below your line, you walk away. Your BATNA is the line, and it holds firm.
The recruiter's exploding deadline is routed out on purpose. Pressure informs the counter but must never drive the decision.

# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet

## Context
- Target role: Junior ML Engineer
- Feedback source: recruiter screen, 2026-06-18
- Feedback (verbatim): "Project looks fine, but I can't tell what YOU decided."

## Diagnosed gap
- NOT a detail-volume problem. Unattributed evidence: claim has no owned decision.

## Rejected quick-patch
- "Add a longer README + more screenshots" -> more words, still no owned tradeoff.

## Rewritten portfolio claim (role-targeted, artifact-linked)
- "Chose batch over streaming ingestion to hit a 6h freshness SLO at 1/5 the infra cost;
   proof: benchmarks/ingestion_ab.md + the cost table in README#tradeoffs."

## STAR interview story
- S: nightly recs were 30h stale.  T: cut to <6h without new infra budget.
- A: A/B'd batch vs streaming; batch met SLO at 1/5 cost; I owned that call.
- R: freshness 30h -> 5h; write-up in benchmarks/ingestion_ab.md.

## Resume bullet
- "Cut recommendation staleness 30h -> 5h by choosing batch ingestion over streaming
   after an A/B cost benchmark (1/5 infra cost)."

## Reviewer objection + response
- Q: "Isn't streaming just better?"  A: not under a 6h SLO + fixed budget — benchmark link.

## Repair note (reusable rule)
- Before any portfolio claim: name the tradeoff I OWNED and link the artifact that proves it.

# Writing the defense packet, one section at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real piece of interview or portfolio feedback you have received (or a realistic one) and run a Feedback Retro: log the raw feedback verbatim, name the actual gap it exposed, rewrite the weak proof into a role-targeted portfolio claim, and defend the rewrite against the objection that triggered the feedback. Capture it all in portfolio_story_and_interview_defense_packet.md.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only summarize at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. The feedback is logged verbatim, not paraphrased. If you softened it, you lost the signal — restore the exact words.
# 2. The diagnosed gap is stated in evidence terms (what proof is missing), not emotional terms ('they didn't like it').
# 3. The rewritten portfolio claim names a tradeoff YOU owned and links a specific artifact by path — a reviewer can open it.
# 4. The STAR story and the resume bullet reuse that same claim and artifact, so spoken and written evidence cannot drift.
# 5. A reviewer objection is pre-loaded with an evidence-backed response, and the repair note is a reusable rule, not 'be more specific'.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

RULES = [
    ("evidence-density", ["deeper experience", "more depth", "couldn't go deep",
                           "surface level"], "rebuild story around numbers + artifacts"),
    ("quantified-results", ["impact unclear", "couldn't quantify", "no metrics"],
     "add measured results to claims"),
    ("communication", ["hard to follow", "rambled", "unstructured"],
     "drill decision-first explanation"),
    ("role-fit", ["fit", "different direction", "not aligned"],
     "re-run role targeting"),
]

LOG = [
    ("onsite", "went with a candidate whose deeper experience stood out"),
    ("screen", "impact unclear from the resume bullets"),
    ("onsite", "answers felt surface level in the design round"),
    ("onsite", "strong coding but couldn't go deep on tradeoffs"),
    ("screen", "team going a different direction"),
    ("onsite", "story was hard to follow under questions"),
]


def classify(text, rules):
    low = text.lower()
    for category, keywords, repair in rules:
        if any(k in low for k in keywords):
            return category, repair
    return "unclassified", "needs human read"


def summarize(log, rules):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied career fixtures.
    # Return inspectable evidence; do not invent experience, outcomes, or market data.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

tallies, dominant = summarize(LOG, RULES)
for cat in sorted(tallies):
    print(f"{cat}: {tallies[cat]}")
cat, count, stages = dominant
print(f"dominant gap: {cat} (n={count}, stages: {', '.join(stages)})")
repair = dict((c, r) for c, _, r in RULES).get(cat, "needs human read")
print(f"repair artifact: {repair}")

storyboard.say: Raw feedback enters the loop — a recruiter note, a mock-interview line, a rejection. It's the cheapest signal you'll ever get about your evidence.
Everything hinges on this decision: do you diagnose the actual gap, or do you just react to how the feedback made you feel?
The feelings path grabs a vague patch — you add more words to the same weak bullet without adding any new proof.
No new evidence means the same rejection. Nothing about the artifact changed, so the objection lands again.
And it loops — wasted. The feedback re-enters, you feel it again, and burn the cheapest signal you had.
The retro path breaks the cycle: diagnose the gap, then rewrite the weak claim so it ties to a named artifact.
You defend the rewrite against the very objection that caused the feedback — pressure-testing the claim, not your intentions.
The output is a reusable defense packet the capstone draws from. The invariant: the retro must change the artifact.

career-capstone.text: Final round, the hiring manager leans in: 'You wrote here that you improved reliability — show me exactly how you know that, and what would have proven you wrong.' The candidate who only has a story stalls; the one carrying a packet opens to the artifact link map and wins the room.

This is the synthesis lesson of Interview Career and Portfolio Proof: every skill you built — role targeting, proof rewriting, the resume bullet, the story bank, the technical walkthrough, outreach, and the feedback loop — collapses into one reusable evidence packet. It is the artifact you carry into the recruiter screen, the panel, and the negotiation.

career-capstone.prompt: Two candidates say the exact same sentence: 'I cut our API latency by 60%.' One gets hired, one gets screened out. Before reading on — what does the room actually reward here?
career-capstone.reveal: Not the claim — the evidence behind it. The winner attaches the artifact: the before/after p99 dashboard, the PR that shipped the fix, the load-test transcript, and the one sentence naming what would have proven them wrong ('if the cache had introduced staleness, conversions would have dropped — they held'). The loser has a number with nothing under it. In interviews, a claim and its proof are different objects; the packet is the skill of never letting them travel apart.

# Portfolio Story & Interview Defense Packet

## Target role
Backend engineer, payments — rewards reliability + measured impact

## Portfolio claim (role-targeted)
Cut checkout p99 latency 4.1s -> 0.9s (under the 1s SLO) without data loss.

## Artifact link map (the proof)
- PR #482: async index worker + backfill        (the change)
- Grafana: p99 before/after, 30-day          (the outcome)
- k6 load-test transcript, 2k RPS             (the verification)
- ADR-014: rejected full reindex, why         (the judgment)

## STAR story (story bank, panel-ready)
- S: checkout p99 was 4.1s, SLO 1s, VP wanted it "fixed Friday"
- T: find the real cause, ship inside SLO, zero daytime downtime
- A: framed it, ran cheapest kill-test first, moved indexing async
- R: p99 -> 0.9s, held 30 days, conversions +2.3%

## Resume bullet
Reduced checkout p99 latency 78% (4.1s->0.9s, under SLO) by moving
indexing async; verified with a 2k-RPS load test, zero data loss.

## Selected vs rejected approach
- Selected: async worker + backfill (reversible, off-hours safe)
- Rejected: full synchronous reindex (violated no-daytime-downtime)

## Expected failure (what would prove me wrong)
Stale index serving old prices -> silent conversion loss. Watched for it.

## Reviewer objection + response
Q: "How do you know the 78% held and was not a fluke?"
A: 30-day Grafana panel + k6 transcript, both linked above.

## Repair notes
First draft claimed "improved performance" (vibe). Repaired to a
number tied to PR #482 + the dashboard.

## Capstone connection
Reuse this packet in the mock panel and the outreach message.
steps: Write the expected evidence verdict before executing the practice reference.

Role targeting first: Before any claim, name the role and what it rewards. A payments-reliability role rewards a latency-and-safety story; a growth role would reward a different claim from the same project. The target selects which claims make the cut.
The portfolio claim: Quantified and role-shaped: '4.1s -> 0.9s, under the 1s SLO, no data loss'. Numbers plus the safety property, not 'made checkout faster'.

The artifact link map — the spine: Four artifacts: the change (PR), the outcome (dashboard), the verification (load test), the judgment (ADR). Every later section points here. This is the answer to 'how do you know?'.
STAR from the story bank: Situation, Task, Action, Result — each line traceable to an artifact above. The Result is a number, not an adjective.
The resume bullet: The claim compressed to one line that survives a 6-second recruiter screen: outcome, magnitude, method, verification — all in it.
Expected failure names the risk: 'Stale index -> silent conversion loss.' Naming what would have proven you wrong is what separates a report from a defense.
The objection defense: Anticipate the hostile question and answer it with a link, not a promise. This is the block that wins the final round.
Repair notes — the honest autopsy: 'improved performance' was a vibe; it became a number tied to a PR. Showing the repair proves the skill is yours, not luck.
Change one input across the decision threshold and explain why the recommendation reverses.

A recruiter reads the packet and can restate what you built and how you proved it — without you narrating.

# Writing the packet, one section at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real project you have shipped and assemble the Portfolio Story and Interview Defense Packet: a role-targeted portfolio claim tied to a named artifact, a STAR interview story, a resume bullet, and a live objection response — every claim pointing at inspectable evidence, not adjectives.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the evidence verdict before running the reference.
# 2. Trace every supplied fixture and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only run_gates at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one hostile or boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
# 5. Replace sample claims only with truthful artifacts and measurements you can defend.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Every portfolio claim points to a specific artifact a reviewer could open (a PR, a dashboard, a test transcript, an ADR) — not an adjective. If any claim has no link, cut it or back it.
# 2. The resume bullet quantifies an outcome (magnitude + baseline + method) and ties to the same artifact as the STAR story — no orphan numbers.
# 3. The STAR story's Result is a measured number, not 'much better', and each of S-T-A-R traces to something in the artifact map.
# 4. You have written the one hostile objection ('how do you know that held?') and answered it with a link, not a promise.
# 5. The packet names a target role and the claims are shaped to what that role rewards — not one generic version aimed at everyone.
# 6. Repair notes show at least one claim that started as a vibe and became evidence — proof the skill is yours.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

PACKET = {
    "claims": [
        {"text": "dup charges cut 93%", "artifact": "dashboard-export:45-to-3"},
        {"text": "p95 held under 300ms", "artifact": "loadtest:k6-287ms"},
        {"text": "zero data loss in cutover", "artifact": ""},
    ],
    "star": {"result": "complaints 5/wk to 0 in two months",
              "artifact": "support-dashboard-export"},
    "bullet": "Cut duplicate charges 93% (45/wk to 3/wk), replay report linked",
    "objection": {"question": "how do you know it wasn't the traffic drop?",
                   "response": "replay holds volume constant; report section 3"},
    "rejected": "we considered other options before choosing the dedupe window",
    "verification": "storm replay: 4812 dupes in, 11 out",
}


def has_digit(s):
    return any(ch.isdigit() for ch in s)


def pct_over_100(s):
    for token in s.replace("(", " ").replace(")", " ").split():
        if token.endswith("%"):
            num = token[:-1].lstrip("-+")
            try:
                if float(num) > 100:
                    return True
            except ValueError:
                continue
    return False


def run_gates(packet):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied career fixtures.
    # Return inspectable evidence; do not invent experience, outcomes, or market data.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the career evidence decision")

passed, failed = run_gates(PACKET)
print(f"gates passed: {passed}/6")
for f in failed:
    print(f"HARD FAIL: {f}")
verdict = "SHIP" if not failed else "FIX TONIGHT"
print(f"verdict: {verdict}")
PACKET["claims"][2]["artifact"] = "migration-log:row-counts-matched"
PACKET["rejected"] = "rejected polling because 4-min lag broke the 15s requirement"
passed, failed = run_gates(PACKET)
print(f"after fixes: {passed}/6 — {'SHIP' if not failed else 'FIX TONIGHT'}")

career-capstone.title: The evidence packet — one project, five faces
career-capstone.subtitle: One shipped project feeds five role-facing surfaces; every surface points back at the same artifact ledger. Adjectives and unbacked claims are deliberately kept OUT — a recruiter screens on evidence, not vibes.

legend.label: role targeting + the artifact ledger (the spine)
the objection defense — 'how do you know?'
unbacked adjectives, kept out on purpose

storyboard.say: It starts with one thing that is real: a shipped project. That single artifact is what every claim in your packet will trace back to.
The shipped project produces an artifact ledger — the commits, dashboards, and metrics a reviewer could actually open and check.
Role targeting sits above the ledger, selecting which claims to surface — you don't show everything, you show what this specific role rewards.
From that one ledger, three writing surfaces get backed at once: the quantified resume bullet, the STAR story, and the technical walkthrough.
The fourth face is the ledger answering 'how do you know?' — objection defense, so the panel's hardest question has a link you can open.
The guardrail: adjectives alone must not leak into the resume. A recruiter screens on evidence a reviewer could open, not on vibes.
One project, five faces, one ledger underneath. The invariant holds: no claim without evidence — that's the packet you carry into the room.
